The browser error is Google OAuth JS origin rejection (Error 400: origin_mismatch), which is governed by the Google OAuth client allowlist in Google Cloud Console, not by Terraform's authorized_domains setting. No repo code change yet; next step is to verify that the OAuth client registered in GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID has https://www.dendritestories.co.nz as an authorized JavaScript origin (and apex if users can reach it directly).

title: Rank 4: add permission-aware portable research service boundary
description:
Parent spec: https://app.notion.com/p/3fb700af-c301-8188-a864-d9e5f57f6b75. Follow-up to the offline reuse fixture dadeto-6ncq.

Hypothesis: a small pure-core service that calls injected bundle readers and writers with AllowEffects can connect bounded evidence-context retrieval and validated V1 experiment submission to the V3 portable format without importing runtime I/O. A fake in-memory adapter and deterministic replay are sufficient to prove the boundary before selecting production storage.

Minimal slice: add createInterpretabilityResearchServiceV1 with permission-first readContext and submitExperiment methods. Inject loadBundle(allowEffects), saveBundle(allowEffects, json), and V1/V2 schema adapters. Read imports/validates the portable bundle and delegates to bounded V1 context retrieval. Submit loads/validates the current bundle, atomically appends the validated experiment/evidence/edges, exports and validates a V3 bundle, then invokes saveBundle only on complete success. Every injected storage operation receives the same AllowEffects token. Test with an in-memory fake adapter, fallback-capable schema test double, and the pinned deterministic replay; prove token forwarding, bounded context reads, persisted portable round trip, and no save after invalid submission.

Acceptance evidence: focused Jest service tests pass; `npm run tsdoc:check`, `git diff --check`, `npm run check`, and exact-head Full Check pass; `npm run agents:reuse-report` accepts the retrospective/event; pushed commit and Notion Rank 4 update are recorded.

title: Diagnose credential leakage in sonar issue dumps
description: gitleaks reported ~930 generic API keys in sonar_issues.json, reports/sonar/sonar_issues.json, and reports/sonar/issues.json. Trace how those snapshots are generated, why the secrets are captured (e.g., exported Sonar payloads) and whether the generator can produce sanitized data instead of raw credentials.

comments.author: matthew.heard
comments.text: Diagnosis: gitleaks only catches the Sonar issue key strings (e.g., "AZdY2ZAU-...") that live in the exported JSON, not a real API key. Those dumps are sourced from  (calls  with the PAT supplied via  and writes ) and from ❌ Docker is installed but the daemon is not running or accessible. (runs SonarScanner, then writes  via another  call). Every issue object contains a  field that starts with , so gitleaks sees it as a generic API key pattern even though it is just Sonar’s issue identifier. The same applies to the legacy  snapshot noted in the report: it would have held the identical data. No committed file actually stores the PAT itself, but the exported issue keys look like secrets. Next step is to decide whether we keep or remove these JSON snapshots (and if kept, replace the  values or omit that field) so gitleaks stops flagging the repo.

comments.author: matthew.heard
comments.text: Clarified diagnosis: `reports/sonar/issues.json` is written by `src/scripts/get-sonar-issues.sh` after fetching `/api/issues/search` from SonarCloud (auth is supplied via the environment-provided `SONAR_TOKEN`). Every object contains a `key` value such as `AZdY2ZAU-gf5lI6Tlo09`, which is the Sonar issue identifier, and gitleaks flags those `AZ…` strings as “generic API keys” even though no secret is stored there. The other snapshots mentioned in the report (the legacy `sonar_issues.json` plus any `reports/sonar/issues-<timestamp>.json` data emitted by `src/scripts/run-sonar.sh`) are generated the same way and therefore carry identical issue IDs that trigger the same false positive. Nothing in the repo actually commits the token itself; the API calls use locally provided credentials and the exported JSON only carries readonly identifiers. Next step is deciding whether to drop these snapshots or scrub/omit their `key` fields (tracked in `dadeto-94s.2`) so gitleaks stops warning about them.

title: THREEFOLD: model small-world water transfer
description: Rank 3 THREEFOLD backlog, milestone 4 small-world content. Hypothesis: a deterministic hydraulic solver with SI-unit chamber geometry can provide physically grounded water transfer and conserve water volume, independent of rendered scale. Minimal slice: implement a pure core module for two rectangular chambers and one controllable port; use Torricelli flow, cap transfer at source volume and hydrostatic equalization, and preserve identical physical outcomes across the nine rendered scales. Tests: open-port downhill flow, closed port, equal head, reversed direction, volume conservation, port-sill limit, and unchanged output when view scale changes while the same physical input is retained. title: Tighten moderation/authedFetch signatures
description:
The tsdoc:check output now highlights several overload/type mismatches inside `src/core/browser/moderation/authedFetch.js` (after `checkJs`/`noImplicitAny` were re-enabled):

- lines 15-44: `Object.fromEntries` is passed a function that returns `HeadersIterator<[string,string]>`, which is currently typed too loosely for `tsc`.
- lines 66-96: options/responses are treated as bare `object`s, so `ok`, `status`, and `json` are marked as missing.

The helper should declare the exact headers/resolver shapes in JSDoc so `tsdoc:check` sees the runtime structure and stop complaining about the iterator + missing fields. Guard the error path so the compiler knows `Error` instances have a `status` when they are used like one.

Acceptance criteria:
* The iterator passed to `Object.fromEntries` has a callable signature that satisfies `Iterable<readonly [PropertyKey, any]>`.
* The `fetch` options/response/resolver signatures include the `ok`, `status`, and `json` properties needed by the helper.
* Any explicit `Error` usage is narrowed before accessing `status` so `tsc` stops flagging the invalid property.

title: Require AllowEffects for mark-variant-dirty HTTP responses
description: The cloud response adapter already requires AllowEffects, but runMarkVariantDirty adapts it back into a callback with no permission parameter and mints a capability separately per response. The core HTTP handler and response helper signatures therefore do not require explicit effect permission. Replace this with a fresh request-boundary capability forwarded through every response path, including verifyAdmin denials, and preserve the external HTTPS handler signature. Acceptance: focused tests prove response adapters receive the request's capability for success, validation/auth errors, and mutation failures; no startup capability is captured; npm run tsdoc:check, npm run check, npm run build:cloud, generated syntax checks, retrospective, evidence, and push pass. Hypothesis: making the response effect mandatory at the core handler boundary will expose all missing forwarding through type/lint errors and remove hidden capability minting from response callbacks.
close_reason: Request-scoped AllowEffects is explicit through mark-variant-dirty auth, response, mutation, and log paths; all loop gates passed.

title: Suppress unhandled Google sign-in rejection in admin auth
description: Google Identity callback was bubbling Firebase auth failures into an unhandled rejection, which triggered Error Reporting for a client-side sign-in path. Catch the callback promise, log the failure, and keep the bootstrap from rejecting.
close_reason: Handled the Google Identity callback rejection and verified npm run check

comments.author: Matt Heard
comments.text: Loop contract: query log insertId fjqee0esogfg, identify the emitted error, and patch the admin sign-in path so the callback no longer leaks an unhandled rejection. Acceptance: the targeted browser tests and full npm run check pass; artifact: src/core/browser/admin-core.js, test/core/browser/admin/core.test.js, notes/agents/2026-07-05T17-01-56Z-google-signin-unhandled-rejection.md.

title: Resolve author regeneration by author uuid field
description: The admin author form sends the published author UUID, but production authors documents use random document IDs and store the UUID in the uuid field. Update the endpoint to query authors where uuid equals the supplied UUID, mark the matched document dirty, test, pass checks, push, and trigger gcp-prod.

comments.author: Matt Heard
comments.text: 2026-07-20 evidence: fixed v1 Firestore trigger runtime binding to process.env.DATABASE_ID in commit 61052abe2f; focused cloud tests 42 passed, tsc/lint passed. gcp-prod run 29706233842 applied render_author successfully, but workflow conclusion was failure because earlier Import existing Firestore database step emitted write EPIPE. Production verification write was denied with Firestore REST 403, so an authenticated admin-page click is still required to confirm prod-render-author logs.

title: Use merge writes for moderator docs
description: Firestore writes to moderators/{uid} are currently split across assignment and reputation recalculation paths. Both use set() without merge, so one workflow can erase fields written by the other.
acceptance_criteria: Assignment and reputation writes both use set(..., { merge: true }); focused tests assert the merge option; repo quality gates are run before close.

comments.author: Matt Heard
comments.text: Hypothesis: switching moderator document writes to set(..., { merge: true }) in assignment and reputation recalculation prevents field clobbering. Acceptance evidence: focused tests for assign-moderation-job and recalculate-moderator-reputation assert the merge option; next gate is npm run check.

title: Add a read-only Atlas portable bundle viewer
description: Rank 4 UI slice. Hypothesis: the validated core import, bounded context query, and typed presenter are not reachable from a browser, so researchers cannot inspect competing hypotheses and evidence. Bundle data stays in browser memory; no cloud storage, authentication, writes, uploads, or inference. Add the browser runtime wiring for injected Zod outside core, and static copy support only for the required core interpretability modules and pinned Zod runtime. Unit tests for the viewer controller must inject the schema adapter/test double and must not import or require Zod. Cheapest evaluator: focused controller tests; then static build output checks and npm run check. Acceptance evidence: viewer tests, build verifies /atlas plus required modules were copied, npm run check, durable UI harness/failure-mode note, Rank 4 Notion update, pushed commit. No bundle data is sent to a server or persisted. Unit tests use injected schemas and pass without actual Zod. Build output contains the Atlas page, core interpretability modules, and Zod runtime. title: Require AllowEffects for render-variant core logging
description: The render-variant entrypoint wraps a tokenless consoleError callback around bindEffectBoundary and injects it through createCloudRenderInstanceBuilder into src/core. The external logger adapter requires AllowEffects, but the core-injected function does not expose the permission parameter, so core can cause logging without explicitly forwarding the capability. Hypothesis: making the core logger permission-first and threading the request capability through render error handling removes this hidden effect seam. Acceptance: core logger types and all call sites require and forward AllowEffects; the external render boundary mints one fresh capability for the logging command; tests prove exact capability forwarding for renderer errors; no startup token is captured; npm run tsdoc:check, npm run check, npm run build:cloud, generated syntax checks, retrospective, Beads evidence, and push pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: Document presenter DOM helpers
description:
The first batch of tsdoc failures now falls inside the presenter helpers:

- `src/core/browser/presenters/battleshipSolitaireClues.js` reports dozens of missing properties/implicit anys (`rowClues`, `colClues`, `Array<T>` generics, unnamed parameter types).
- `src/core/browser/presenters/ticTacToeBoard.js` and `src/core/browser/tags.js` also show `tsc` treating DOM helpers as plain `object` and reporting implicit `any` parameters (e.g., `position`, `player`, `event`).

We need to declare shared DOM helper typedefs (`DOMHelpers`, `TextHelpers`, etc.) and annotate each exported helper so the compiler knows the exact properties and removes the `unknown`/`object` errors. In particular, the presenter functions should accept typed `options` with `rowClues`, `colClues`, and the DOM `container` helper should list `createElement`/`setTextContent`/`addEventListener` so uses of those properties stop being flagged.

Acceptance criteria:
* Each presenter helper has a documented parameter shape (e.g., `@typedef {object} BattleshipCluePayload`) that lists the needed arrays/fields.
* The DOM helper objects passed into the presenters expose explicit members instead of being inferred as `object`.
* The `tsdoc:check` run that currently produces these errors no longer reports them (the rest of the log can still fail elsewhere).
